passage:
When Tenzin was nine, his parents lit up only when a test came home with a big number. His father Yogesh would say, "Ninety-eight! Show everyone." When a paper came home with a lower score, Yogesh went quiet and turned the television up. Tenzin began to slip the weaker papers into the bottom of his bag.

By fifteen, his teacher Zubin held up Tenzin's notebook in class. "Look at this. Not a single crossing-out." The whole class clapped, and Tenzin felt warm and safe. He started rewriting whole pages when he made one blot, staying up until midnight, because a flawed page felt like a way of losing that clapping. On the day of a class test he scored lower than usual, went pale and told nobody.

At dinner Yogesh asked how school had gone and Tenzin said, "Fine." The fear stayed under the word.

qa.q: What did Zubin hold up in front of the class when Tenzin was fifteen?
qa.a: Zubin held up Tenzin's notebook and pointed out that it had no crossing-out.

qa.q: How does the way Yogesh responds at home connect to Tenzin's rewriting of pages at fifteen?
qa.a: At nine Tenzin learns that his parents light up for big numbers and go quiet otherwise, so he hides weak papers; at fifteen the praise for flawless work makes being perfect feel like the price of safety, so he rewrites pages and hides a poor test.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when he said school was fine at dinner?
qa.a: Tenzin was afraid and ashamed of the lower score, hiding it because it might cost him the warmth he gets for being flawless.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do to make Tenzin feel safe about mistakes?
qa.a: Yogesh could respond warmly to weaker papers too, asking what Tenzin learned, so that love does not depend on the number.

grounding: Perfectionism from a parent who responds only to marks to a teenager who learns that praise and safety come with flawless work, hiding the fear underneath.
